Yeah, hi. Well, honestly, it's... it's just been a lot lately. I work down at the distribution warehouse—I've been a shipping and inventory clerk there for years, you know, just doing my job, keeping my head down, making sure things get where they need to go. But a little while ago, they decided to make me the acting workflow lead. Which, you know, sounds like a good thing on paper, but ever since that happened, I just... I don't even know who I am right now. 

I mean, I literally walk through the double doors into the warehouse and my shoulders are already up to my ears. I'm just so tense before I even clock in. And I find myself snapping at the guys over the stupidest little SAP errors—like, somebody puts in the wrong bin number in the software, which happens all the time, it's just part of the job, but suddenly I'm just biting their heads off about it. 

And the worst part is, I'm actually missing my own cycle-count deadlines. I never miss cycle counts. I've always been the guy management relies on to get the inventory numbers right, and now I'm just dropping the ball. It's just... it's exhausting. By the time my shift is over, I go home and I am just completely drained. Like, bone-tired. I used to play pickup basketball a couple of nights a week, or at least sit down and work on my sketches—I took some art classes back in college, so I've always liked to draw to unwind—but now? I just sit there. I don't have the energy for basketball, I don't even look at my sketchpad... I just feel like this whole lead position thing has completely derailed me, and I don't know how to fix it.

Sadness? Um... I don't know if sadness is the right word for it. It's not like I'm sitting around crying or anything, you know? I'm not, like, weeping into my cereal bowl in the morning. It just feels like I'm stuck in this... this weird limbo where I'm not the guy I used to be, but I'm definitely not cut out to be this new guy either. So yeah, maybe there is some hopelessness there, just feeling like I'm trapped in this situation that I didn't even really ask for, and not knowing how to get back to when things were just... normal.

Avoiding? No, I mean... I wouldn't say I'm avoiding anything. If anything, I'm probably staring at it all too much. I wish I could just go hide in the back by the empty pallets sometimes, you know? But no, I'm right there in the thick of it every single shift.

I hate it, my stomach is in knots the whole time, but I still do it. I stand up there with my clipboard and read off the inbound freight expectations and the priority outbound shipments. And then there's the SAP software stuff. I mentioned the bin location errors earlier. I'm not putting off fixing them, I'm actually sitting right there at my desk, staring at my dual monitors, trying to track down exactly who scanned what into the wrong aisle. Like yesterday, we had this massive discrepancy in Aisle 4 with some automotive parts, and I spent three hours just digging through the digital logs trying to reconcile the manifest. 

So, no, I'm not hiding in the bathroom or shoving paperwork into a drawer or anything like that. I'm trying to do all of it. I'm trying to do my old duties and all this new acting lead stuff, like the shift-end reports that Dave—he's the floor manager—expects in his inbox by 3:30 PM sharp. I'm sitting there trying to get it all done. It's just... like I said before, I'm missing my deadlines on the cycle counts, not because I'm avoiding them, but because I'm just so overwhelmed and bogged down by every little thing now. I'm facing it all head-on, I'm just... I'm just doing a really terrible job at it now because my brain is just spinning the whole time. So yeah, no avoidance. Just a lot of struggling while I'm doing it.

Well, let's see... it's been about four months now. Yeah, four months. It all started right when they decided to restructure the warehouse. You know how corporate is, always trying to streamline things, right? So they took the inbound receiving team and the outbound shipping team, and they merged the inventory control for both into one massive department. I had just finished my sandwich, and he calls me in and says, "Hey, we're making you the acting workflow lead for this new merged team." He made it sound like this huge opportunity, you know? Like I was finally getting recognized for my six years of hard work. But really, they just didn't want to hire a new manager, so they dumped it on me. "Acting" lead, right? Which basically means all the responsibility and none of the pay bump. 

So yeah, for the last four months, ever since that Tuesday when they merged the teams and slapped that title on me, it's just been this constant, grinding tension. Day one, I was already behind because they didn't even train me on the new SAP modules for the outbound side. I just had to figure it out while managing fifteen guys who were just as confused as I was. Four months of waking up with my chest tight, four months of dreading the morning huddle, four months of just feeling like I'm drowning in cycle counts and bin errors. It feels a lot longer, to be honest. It feels like it's been a year. But yeah, chronologically, it's been exactly four months since the merger and the promotion... if you can even call it that.

It's just... like I said before, I'm missing my deadlines on the cycle counts, not because I'm avoiding them, but because I'm just so overwhelmed and bogged down by every little thing now. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Detached? Like, like I'm floating outside my body or zoning out or something? No, man, I wish. If I could just float away from that warehouse floor for five minutes and not feel any of it, I'd take it in a heartbeat. But no, it's the exact opposite. I am so painfully aware of every single thing happening around me. I don't feel detached at all. I feel like I'm hyper-attached to every little disaster going on in that building. 

Like, just the noise alone, right? If I was detached, maybe I wouldn't hear the constant beeping of the forklifts backing up. That loud, piercing beep echoing off the corrugated steel roof all shift long. Or the sound of the RF barcode scanners—that sharp little chirp every time a pallet gets logged into the system. I hear every single one of them. I feel the hard concrete floor right through the soles of my steel-toe boots. My neck aches from hunching over at that desk staring at those dual monitors, trying to fix the SAP errors I told you about. I am one hundred percent physically and mentally trapped right there in the middle of it all. 

There's no zoning out for me. I can't even daydream or disconnect for a second. Because the minute I try to just stare off into space and catch my breath, Dave is walking by checking on the shift-end reports, or one of the guys from the inbound team is tapping me on the shoulder asking why the bay door on dock four is jammed again. So, no, I'm definitely not detached from myself or the warehouse. I'm just... I'm just marinating in it, you know? Every single second of that shift, I am completely, miserably aware that I am sitting there drowning in this acting lead job. I never get the luxury of tuning it out.

Sleep? Oh man, don't even get me started on sleep. I mean, honestly, what even is sleep anymore? It's like this mythical thing I used to do back before Dave made me the acting workflow lead. Because no, I haven't been sleeping well at all. I haven't had a decent night's sleep in four months.

Wait, did the outbound crew actually finish loading trailer 412, or did they leave it sitting on the dock again? And then I start thinking about tomorrow. I start dreading the morning huddle. I start picturing Dave walking up with his clipboard, asking about the cycle counts. I literally rehearse conversations in my head, trying to figure out what I'm going to say when he asks why we're behind again. 

And before I know it, I look over at the alarm clock, and it's 2:00 AM. Then it's 3:30 AM. And my alarm is set for 5:15 AM so I can get up, shower, make coffee, and beat the traffic on I-95. So by the time I actually drift off, it's just this shallow, restless kind of sleep where I'm dreaming about spreadsheets and forklifts. And then the alarm goes off, and I feel worse than when I went to bed. I'm just dragging myself out from under the covers, chugging coffee, and trying to function on maybe two hours of actual sleep. It's miserable. It's just... it's a vicious cycle, you know? I'm too tired to do my job right, but I'm too stressed about doing my job wrong to actually get any sleep. So yeah, trouble sleeping is definitely an understatement.
